expected_answer_points: Default argument values are evaluated once, when the def statement executes at definition time, not on each call; the same list object is bound as the default (retrievable via the function's __defaults__).
Because append() mutates that single shared list in place, items persist across calls that rely on the default, so unrelated conversations accumulate each other's messages.
Correct fix is the sentinel pattern: default to None (or a unique sentinel) and allocate a fresh list inside the body when the argument was not supplied.

Explains that `if history is None: history = []` creates a new list per call, and that `is None` is preferable to a truthiness check like `history or []` which mishandles a legitimately-passed empty/falsy value.
(a) Identifies that even with the None-sentinel fix, a caller-supplied list is still mutated in place (aliasing); to avoid side-effecting the caller's object, copy it (e.g. history = list(history)).
Notes that if None is itself a valid argument value, a private sentinel object (_MISSING = object()) should be used instead of None.
(b) Acknowledges the shared-default persistence can be (ab)used as a cache/memo but should be made explicit; mentions linters flag it (ruff/flake8-bugbear B006 or pylint W0102).
common_pitfalls: Claims default arguments are re-evaluated on every call and therefore concludes the code 'should' reset each time — misdiagnosing the mechanism entirely instead of recognizing the once-at-definition evaluation.

Uses `history = history or []` and calls it equivalent to `is None`, missing that truthiness silently discards a deliberately-passed empty list and mishandles other falsy inputs.
Applies the None-sentinel fix but asserts it is now fully side-effect-free, overlooking that a caller-supplied list is still mutated in place (aliasing).

reference_answer:
This is Python's default-argument evaluation model, not a logic error. A default value is evaluated exactly once, when the `def` statement runs at definition/import time, and the resulting object is stored on the function itself (in `build_messages.__defaults__`). There is therefore a single list shared by every call that relies on the default. Because `history.append(...)` mutates that list in place, each request that omits `history` appends onto the same object, so later 'fresh' conversations already hold earlier messages.

Fix with the sentinel pattern:

```python
def build_messages(user_msg, history=None):
    if history is None:
        history = []
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_msg})
    return history
```

A new list is allocated per call, so no state leaks. Prefer `is None` over `history or []`: truthiness would also discard a deliberately-passed empty list and mishandle other falsy inputs.

(a) No. Even after the fix, when a caller passes their own list the function still mutates it in place (aliasing); the caller sees the appended message. If that side effect is unwanted, copy first: `history = list(history)`. If `None` is itself a valid value, use a private sentinel `_MISSING = object()` instead.

(b) The shared, persistent default is occasionally exploited as a cheap per-function cache/memo, but an explicit module-level dict is clearer and linters (ruff/flake8-bugbear B006, pylint W0102) flag the mutable default by default.
